Op-Ed: “Space Belongs to Everyone,” Say People Who Have Never Tried to File a Launch Permit

There’s a certain romance to the phrase “space resources belong to all humanity.” It sounds noble, poetic, and just vague enough to make you feel morally superior while contributing absolutely nothing to the rocket fuel budget.

These critics—let’s call them the Celestial Commons Enthusiasts—insist that if America so much as picks up a shiny rock in orbit, it should immediately convene a global committee, host three rounds of multilingual hearings, and then distribute asteroid dust in equal portions to every person on Earth, ideally via artisanal, carbon-neutral envelopes.

Because nothing says “progress” like turning the universe into a group project.

The “All Humanity” Ownership Model (A.K.A. The World’s Least Practical HOA)

When someone says “space belongs to everyone,” what they usually mean is:

  1. Everyone owns it
  2. No one can use it
  3. The people who actually go there should ask permission from the people who don’t

It’s like declaring your neighbor’s backyard pool a “shared resource of the entire cul-de-sac,” then showing up with a clipboard demanding equitable chlorine distribution while the neighbor is still digging the hole.

Critics talk about space like it’s a public library. In reality, it’s more like the world’s most hostile construction site, where the air is trying to kill you, the temperature is a prank, and your “free sample” of asteroid comes with a six-figure launch bill.

But sure—tell me again how the ethical thing is to leave it all untouched until Luxembourg and 193 other stakeholders agree on a vibes-based allocation framework.

Treaties: Because Nothing Speeds Innovation Like 1970s Paperwork

We also hear a lot about international treaties restricting national claims, usually delivered in the solemn tone reserved for sacred texts and parking enforcement.

Look, treaties have their place. But when critics cite them like they’re cosmic commandments—“Thou shalt not mine, lest thou anger the Outer Space Accord”—it’s hard not to notice that many of these rules were written when “space activity” meant two guys in a tin can seeing what happens.

The world has changed a bit since then. We now have reusable rockets, private launch providers, and enough high-resolution satellite imagery to locate a lost golf ball on Mars (allegedly).

So when someone argues that resource extraction must be frozen until every nation on Earth agrees on a comprehensive governance regime, what they’re really saying is:

> “Please stop the future until the bureaucracy catches up.”

That’s not caution. That’s a filibuster in a spacesuit.

The Critics’ Favorite Fantasy: The United Nations Asteroid Distribution Center

Let’s play out the “belongs to all humanity” approach.

An American company brings back a platinum-rich asteroid chunk. Immediately, the global community demands it be shared “fairly.” Naturally, this requires:

  • A UN subcommittee on extraterrestrial equity
  • A working group on asteroid naming conventions
  • A conference to ensure the asteroid’s cultural heritage is respected
  • A binding resolution condemning anyone who smiles about it too much

Then, after 12 years, the committee issues a 900-page report concluding that more research is needed, and also the asteroid should be returned to space to avoid setting a precedent.

Meanwhile, the only people who actually did the thing are told they’re greedy, reckless, and probably colonizers of the Kuiper Belt.

“Unilateral Exploitation” vs. “Everyone Benefits Eventually”

Here’s the part critics always skip: someone has to build the capability first. That means:

  • R&D
  • launch risk
  • engineering
  • supply chains
  • capital
  • years of work with a nontrivial chance of turning your payload into modern art scattered across the upper atmosphere

Then, when it works, the critics show up like it’s a potluck and they brought a pamphlet.

And what’s truly adorable is the assumption that not doing anything is more ethical than doing something. As if leaving resources untouched forever is a morally superior outcome—like we’re preserving asteroids for future generations to also not use.

Yes, let’s treat space resources like a museum exhibit: “Please do not touch the nickel-iron. It belongs to everyone, meaning it must remain functionally available to no one.”

The Real Naivety: Thinking “Common Heritage” Prevents Competition

The most counterproductive part of the opposition is the belief that declaring space a “shared heritage” magically prevents conflict.

In practice, it often does the opposite: if nobody can establish clear rights to extract, invest, and trade, then you don’t get peaceful development—you get ambiguity. And ambiguity is what turns resource frontiers into geopolitical games of chicken.

If critics truly want stability, they should want transparent rules that actually align incentives with reality: you invest, you extract, you profit, you trade, others benefit through markets, technology spillover, and cheaper materials.

Instead, they propose the cosmic equivalent of banning farms so nobody feels left out of the harvest.

A Modest Proposal for the “All Humanity” Crowd

If space resources belong to all humanity, great. Here’s a simple plan:

  • Everyone chips in for the rockets.
  • Everyone shares the risk.
  • Everyone gets a vote on mission design.
  • Everyone helps pay for the insurance.
  • Everyone is welcome to contribute expertise, capital, or hardware.

No?

Then perhaps we can admit the truth: “all humanity” is often just a rhetorical costume for “the people doing the work should be constrained by the people who aren’t.”

Which is a lovely sentiment—right up until you realize that the universe doesn’t run on sentiments.

It runs on delta‑v.
